items.summary: feat(update): Git installs update through prepared releases and a resident launcher (#203194) ## Problem A Git install updates in place under the running Gateway, through a managed-service handoff helper. When the new build does not start, recovery depends on that helper and on the old updater that is already installed, so a failed update can leave the Gateway down or stuck in `update-recovery-pending`. ## Change Git installs now update through prepared releases and a resident launcher: 1. `update.run`, `openclaw update` and automatic updates admit the run, resolve the target and run preflight (Node engine, required tools, disk space, container installs refused before any change). 2. The next release is built beside the running one (`git worktree add --detach`, then the target's install and build). The running checkout is not changed. 3. `openclaw update check-release` runs the new code offline against the current config and state and reports broken plugin or config surfaces. It does not migrate state. 4. `openclaw update plugins` runs from the published release: the existing plugin maintenance owner (`updatePluginsAfterCoreUpdate`), with the new core's code and version. A plugin problem, or a target too old to have the command, is recorded as a `plugins` step with a next action and never fails the update. An already-current install still runs it from the serving code and restarts a running Gateway when plugins changed (`docs/install/updating.md`). 5. The release is published as a pending trial, and the Gateway restarts with a process-replacing reason. 6. The launcher switches the release link at the next child start, counts attempts, commits the trial when the new Gateway is ready, and otherwise rolls back and starts the previous release. 7. The Gateway that starts after the switch (new on success, old after a rollback) finishes the run and sends the outcome to a requester that received the start notice. Routing: - `update.run` reads the install kind from the existing install-status owner (`resolveStartupInstallStatus`). `update-run.ts` wraps `update.run`; `update.ts` is unchanged and still serves package installs. - `openclaw update` branches after `prepareUpdateCommand`, so every existing refusal (external supervisor, host-owned, immutable, system package owner, interrupted update) applies first. A requested non-dev channel on a Git checkout still switches it to a package through the existing flow, and `--dry-run` keeps the existing preview. - Package installs move to this path in the next change, which also deletes the old Git machinery that this PR leaves unused. Converting an existing install: - The old entry points of a converted install (`openclaw.mjs`, `dist/index.js`) forward to the release launcher through a marker beside the tree. Existing service definitions and PATH shims keep working without a rewrite. - A first update driven by an older installed updater still migrates state as it does today. Released updaters require migrated state: 23 stable and 6 extended-stable tags contain that check. Fixes found by the real-install runs below, each a separate commit: - `openclaw update --sha` now sends the tracked upstream that the protocol requires. - The new path restarts with `update.run` / `update.auto`, so the process is replaced instead of restarted in place. - A Gateway started by the launcher leaves its update successor to the launcher instead of spawning one outside it. - Preflight skips dangling symlinks in agent homes, such as Codex `arg0` shims, when it sizes state databases. - `check-release` writes its JSON result to stdout. - Plain `openclaw update` keeps following the run while the restarting Gateway refuses connections with a retryable HTTP 503. Before, it exited 1 although the update succeeded. Accepted edge cases: - After `openclaw update` runs in a Git checkout, `openclaw.mjs` and `dist/index.js` in that checkout run the current release. A developer who edits the source of a checkout they also update from runs the release, not their edits. - A stop request handled inside a launcher child exits with code 0, and the launcher starts the child again. A stop through the service manager stops the launcher and its child. - On a Gateway with no service manager, the first update from a released version does not restart it. The released updater does this, and says so. - Package updates now read the install status twice per request: once to route, once in the old handler. - After a rollback, the previous release runs with plugins maintained for the new core. A plugin that cannot load stays off for that boot, as the plugin docs describe. - `openclaw update --accept-capabilities` reaches plugin maintenance when the CLI prepares the release itself (`--no-restart`, or no Gateway answering). Through a running Gateway, `update.run` has no field for it, so a plugin that needs consent is reported with its `openclaw plugins update` next action. Carrying the flag through `update.run` is a protocol change and follows separately. - `openclaw update` run from a different checkout than the one the configured local Gateway serves updates the Gateway's installation, not the invoking checkout. Binding the request to the checkout needs a protocol field and follows with `--accept-capabilities`. ## Evidence Real install on macOS (Apple silicon). Isolated HOME, state, config and port, a foreground Gateway, no launchd service. Every candidate was built from `git archive` of its commit; the final candidate is this branch's head before review. | Step | Run status | Trial | Served after | Health | |---|---|---|---|---| | 2026.11.6 → A (released updater) | succeeded | (old path) | A, after a recorded manual start | 200 / 200 | | A → B′ (B′ fails at startup) | failed, `new build failed to start` | rolled-back, 2 attempts | A, as the launcher's child | 200 / 200 | | A → B | succeeded | committed, 1 attempt | B, as the launcher's child | 200 / 200 | | B → C | succeeded | committed, 1 attempt | C, as the launcher's child | 200 / 200 | - The same launcher process stayed the parent through every replacement. The previous release was kept after each commit. - Phase times (seconds), from the persisted run steps: | Step | Staging (build) | Validating | Restarting | Total | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | A → B′ (rollback) | 192.5 | 0.8 | 29.2 | 222.7 | | A → B | 195.7 | 1.1 | 32.9 | 229.8 | | B → C | 201.6 | 0.9 | 36.9 | 239.5 | - `check-release` on a copy of a real state directory (Linux, no network): exit 0 in 3.0 s, 187 surfaces checked, shared state schema 40 → 40, agent databases 43 → 43. Plugin maintenance, real install on macOS (isolated, foreground Gateway, a real third-party npm plugin `@martian-engineering/lossless-claw` served through a scratch registry proxy that advertises 1.1.1, then the real latest 1.2.0): | Case | Run | `plugins` step | Plugin | Gateway | |---|---|---|---|---| | Core update through the new path | succeeded, trial committed (1 attempt) | completed | 1.1.1 → 1.2.0 | one restart into the new release | | Already current, plugin outdated | skipped / already-current | completed | 1.1.1 → 1.2.0 | restarted | | Already current, nothing to change | skipped / already-current | completed | unchanged | no restart | | Already current, registry returns HTTP 503 | skipped / already-current | completed, detail names the plugin and its `openclaw plugins update` retry | kept 1.1.1 | no restart; CLI prints "Plugin notes: …" | | Already current, `--no-restart` | skipped / already-current | completed | 1.1.1 → 1.2.0 | same process, no restart | - An earlier head counted a `warning` result as a failed step with no message; the run above found it and the fix is in this PR. - A run with `--timeout 1` showed the CLI calling a still-running update "Update failed: unknown reason". The fix ("The update did not finish in time. Run `openclaw update status` to see it.") is covered by `src/update/cli.test.ts`; it was not rerun on the real install. Tests: - New: `src/update/*.test.ts` (target, preflight, Git and package preparation, check-release, store, launcher, trial settlement and outcome notice, CLI request shape), plus a launcher-child case in `process-respawn.test.ts`. - The gateway `update*` suites run against package installs. Tests that pinned the old Git handoff, Git preflight delegation, explicit Git targets and foreground parking are deleted. Tests of behavior that package installs still use (notice policy, owner checks, campaign adoption, platform admission) now run on a managed package install. ## Review - `--no-restart` on a Git install now prepares the release in the CLI process instead of asking the Gateway, so the Gateway does not restart. The release starts at the Gateway's next start, and the CLI says so and exits 0, instead of reporting "Updated". - The first conversion creates the `prefix/openclaw` link to the running tree before it writes the forwarding marker. Forwarded commands work between publish and the switch. - The run row is written through the existing asynchronous update-run owner (`update-run-write.async.ts`). The synchronous second writer is deleted, so there is no SQLite work on the Gateway thread. - Rejected: settling trials of the format-1 Git-release launcher (#199706). No released build contains it (not 2026.11.6 `latest`, 2026.10.33 `extended-stable` or 2026.11.10-beta.1 `beta`), and main-only code is not a shipped contract. Only a Git checkout that tracked `main` between 2026-11-17 and this change can have such a trial. - The in-process path (`--no-restart`, or no Gateway answering) uses the requested channel, else the saved `update.channel` (`readUpdateChannelConfig`), else `dev`, as the existing CLI does. The Gateway path passes the checkout's tag and branch facts, as the existing handler does, so a configless checkout on a stable tag stays on stable. - After publishing a Git release, `git worktree repair` records it at its final path, so `git worktree list` and a later `git worktree prune` see the serving release where it is. - `prefix/openclaw` is repointed to the running tree when it does not already resolve there, so a link left from an earlier package install cannot become the rollback target. - Rejected for this PR: carrying the package layout's `lib/node_modules/openclaw` link. That layout belongs to package-release installs, which this PR does not route; the next change moves package installs and owns it. - A new build that exits 78 (it refuses the configuration) during a trial now rolls back like any other failed candidate. Outside a trial, 78 stays terminal. - Rejected again, same reason as the format-1 trial: making `git-install/lib/node_modules/openclaw` follow `prefix/openclaw`. Only the main-only Git-release conversion (#199706) creates that link, and no release contains it. - A Gateway with `OPENCLAW_NO_RESPAWN` set now refuses `update.run` with `restart-unavailable` before anything is recorded or prepared, as the existing handler does. The prepared release starts only in a new process, which that Gateway cannot start. - `openclaw update --timeout ` on a Git install is the overall budget again: it bounds how long the CLI follows the run, reaches the Gateway as `update.run` `timeoutMs`, and target resolution, the release build and plugin maintenance get only what remains of it. Preflight and `check-release` keep their own short bounds. - Rejected again, same reason as the format-1 trial: settling legacy `.trial` records in `stale-install.ts`. Only #199706 writes them; `settleGitReleaseTrial` is in no released build (2026.11.6 `latest`, 2026.10.33 `extended-stable`, 2026.11.10-beta.1 `beta`). - Rejected: routing `--tag` on a Git install to the package flow. The existing Git flow ignores `--tag` ("--tag applies to npm installs only; git updates ignore it"), so the Git route keeps that behavior. - After merging `main`: Control UI and desktop app requests on a Git install show the update in the app instead of the conversation (#203357), through the same `appUpdateNoticePublisher` owner as package installs. - A manual `update.run` on a Git install during a scheduled campaign adopts the campaign through its existing owner: it applies the pinned commit, records `trigger: campaign` with the campaign ID, binds the run, and refuses a mismatched `--sha` or a campaign already applying, as package installs do. - Rejected a third time: settling legacy `.trial` records (same reason as above). - Rejected: restoring the plugin cohort across a trial rollback. Removing the cohort is the approved design (plugins are non-fatal). After a rollback the previous release runs with plugins maintained for the new core; a plugin that cannot load stays off for that boot. Listed under accepted edge cases. - Updating without a Gateway (`--no-restart`, or none answering) reads the checkout's tag and branch facts, as the Gateway route does, so a stable-tag checkout with no saved `update.channel` stays on stable instead of preparing `dev`. - `openclaw update --no-restart --json` no longer prints the human "is ready" line before the JSON result. - Deferred: carrying `--accept-capabilities` through `update.run` (a protocol change); listed under accepted edge cases. - `openclaw update` delegates to `update.run` only when the call targets the configured local Gateway (`isImplicitLocalGatewayTarget`). With `gateway.mode=remote` or a Gateway URL override it prepares this checkout in-process instead of updating the remote installation. - `check-release` and `update plugins` run through the existing process owner (`runCommandWithTimeout` with process-tree termination), so a timeout ends npm and every descendant and waits for them before the step settles. - A linked Git worktree gets the root-level `.openclaw-launcher` marker (its `.git` is a file); only a main working tree uses `.git/openclaw-launcher`. Before, the marker went to the main working tree, so the linked worktree never forwarded. Not covered by a new test: it needs a full release build through publish. - Deferred with `--accept-capabilities`: binding `update.run` to the CLI's checkout. When the configured local Gateway runs another installation than the checkout the CLI runs from, the Gateway updates its own installation. Matching them needs the admitted root in `update.run` (a protocol change). The previous in-place Git updater had the same mismatch: it updated the invoking checkout and restarted the configured service. - A Git install is already current only when the serving build's commit (`resolveLoadedCommitHash`) matches the target, not when the checkout's `HEAD` does. A checkout pulled to the target without a rebuild still runs the old build, so it now prepares the release. An unknown build commit prepares a release too. - The Git route honors `update.run` `restartDelayMs` when it restarts into a prepared release or after changed plugins, as the package route does. ## Merge danger - Two-way door for the code: a revert restores the old Git update path. The forwarder that reads the launcher marker ships in this change, so after a revert the checkout's `openclaw.mjs` runs the checkout again and the old updater updates it in place; the `git-install/` prefix is left unused. A revert was not exercised. - One-way parts: a converted install has a `git-install/` prefix with releases, the launcher and a forwarding marker beside the checkout; a revert leaves them in place. No schema, stored-row or protocol version change. - Blast radius: Git installs only (source checkouts updating with `openclaw update`, `update.run` and automatic updates). Package installs keep the existing path. Co-authored-by: Ayaan Zaidi

items.summary: fix(update): name the working Gateway recovery after a shipped pnpm updater leaves it stopped (#203406) * fix(update): name the verified Gateway recovery after a shipped pnpm updater refuses the restart Shipped updaters 2026.11.4 through 2026.11.6 refuse the Gateway restart after a same-schema pnpm update (`service-revalidation-failed`) and leave the Gateway stopped. The verified recovery is `openclaw gateway install --force` followed by `openclaw gateway restart`; `gateway restart` alone fails while the service still names the previous store directory. One module decides that state: on macOS or Linux, the service this pnpm installation owns and may rewrite still names another version's package in the same pnpm home. - Doctor, run by such an updater, prints the pair once when it had to repair the launcher that updater published (the marker of a shipped driver; a fixed one publishes a working launcher). - `openclaw update status` names the pair as the next step for a `service-revalidation-failed` run while the Gateway is not responding. - `openclaw gateway status --deep` names it in the installation drift line while the service is stopped. - The update docs no longer claim that these updaters always hand the restart to the new package. * fix(update): bound the refused-restart lookup and require the owner's verdict - `openclaw update status` reads the live service for the refused-restart recovery through its deadline-bound inspection. - A pruned previous store entry no longer counts as owned by its absence; without the service owner's verdict the readers stay silent. * fix(update): report the refused-restart recovery through the Doctor result and for the right service - Doctor returns the note as an update warning, which shipped updaters render in their final report and record for `openclaw update status`; a successful Doctor's own output is not shown to the user. - Service selectors and the profile survive the service read, and both commands are rendered for the profile the reader runs under. - A version another pnpm global project in the same home still uses is not this installation's previous generation. - The status readers name the recovery only while the service is stopped. * fix(update): name the reinstall only for the run that made the pnpm switch - The status readers require the failed run to have moved the install from the version the stopped service still runs to the active one. - A pruned previous entry has no manifest to prove what it was, so no reader names the reinstall for it; the lexical-path fallback is gone. - `gateway status --deep` reads the run ledger from the preflight state and the service as the caller selected it. - The update guide names the managed-service and ownership conditions.

A hosted endpoint stops logically, so these runtimes never claim a shared-host slot, and a SQLite broker that captured the conservative policy keeps its carriers dedicated. * fix: register the hosted worker start protocol with the export guard * fix: annotate the host engine-selection assertion and mock the history scope close
